foundations.name: Sets, functions & proof
foundations.label: arXiv math.LO · Logic (MSC 03)
foundations.field: mathematical logic and the foundations of mathematics: set theory, proof theory, model theory, computability and their applications
foundations.peopleNote: Six researchers with widely recognised influence on set theory, model theory and formal proof who are still publishing on arXiv.

openQuestions.title: The continuum hypothesis and new axioms
openQuestions.q: Is there an infinite set larger than the natural numbers but smaller than the real numbers?
openQuestions.known: Gödel (1940) and Cohen (1963) showed the usual axioms (ZFC) can neither prove nor refute the continuum hypothesis. The live question is which new axioms mathematicians should accept: forcing axioms such as Martin’s Maximum imply the continuum has size ℵ₂, whereas Woodin’s Ultimate L programme points towards the hypothesis being true.

openQuestions.title: An “ultimate” canonical universe
openQuestions.q: Is there a canonical, fine-structural model of set theory, like Gödel’s L, that is compatible with the strongest large cardinals?
openQuestions.known: Inner models of this kind are known for large cardinals up to roughly Woodin cardinals and somewhat beyond. Woodin’s Ultimate L conjecture predicts such a model exists even for a supercompact cardinal; it remains unproved.

openQuestions.title: Short proofs and NP versus coNP
openQuestions.q: Does every proof system for propositional logic have true statements whose shortest proofs are exponentially long?
openQuestions.known: Cook and Reckhow (1979) showed this holds for every proof system exactly when NP ≠ coNP. Exponential lower bounds are proved for weaker systems such as resolution (Haken, 1985), but the question is open for Frege systems, the standard textbook proof systems.

openQuestions.title: Vaught’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: Can a complete theory in a countable language have more than countably many, but fewer than continuum many, countable models?
openQuestions.known: Vaught (1961) conjectured that it cannot. It is proved for ω-stable theories (Shelah, Harrington and Makkai, 1984) and for o-minimal theories (Mayer, 1988), but remains open in general.

openQuestions.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
openQuestions.q: Is there an algorithm that decides whether a polynomial equation with rational coefficients has a rational solution?
openQuestions.known: Over the integers the answer is no (Matiyasevich, 1970, completing work of Davis, Putnam and Robinson). Over the rationals a Diophantine definition of ℤ inside ℚ would settle it negatively. Until recently such definitions were known only under unproved conjectures; a preprint posted on 12 November 2026 (Burungale) claims an unconditional one, which has not yet been peer reviewed.

openQuestions.title: Tarski’s exponential function problem
openQuestions.q: Is there an algorithm that decides every first-order statement about the real numbers with addition, multiplication and the exponential function?
openQuestions.known: Without the exponential, Tarski showed the answer is yes. Wilkie (1996) proved the theory with exp is model complete, and Macintyre and Wilkie (1996) proved it decidable assuming Schanuel’s conjecture, which is itself unproved.

milestones.title: Not all infinities are equal
milestones.text: Cantor proves the real numbers cannot be listed in a sequence: there are more reals than natural numbers.

milestones.title: Logic becomes a formal language
milestones.text: Frege’s Begriffsschrift introduces quantifiers and the first fully formal system of predicate logic.

milestones.title: Russell’s paradox
milestones.text: The set of all sets that are not members of themselves cannot consistently exist, exposing a flaw in naive set theory.

milestones.title: Axioms for sets
milestones.text: Zermelo publishes axioms for set theory; with later additions by Fraenkel and Skolem these become ZF, the standard foundation.

milestones.title: Incompleteness
milestones.text: Gödel shows any consistent, effectively axiomatised theory containing arithmetic has true statements it cannot prove.

milestones.title: Limits of computation
milestones.text: Church and Turing show there is no general algorithm for deciding first-order validity; Turing’s halting problem is undecidable.

milestones.title: Forcing and independence
milestones.text: Cohen invents forcing and proves the continuum hypothesis cannot be proved from ZFC, complementing Gödel’s 1938 consistency result.

milestones.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem
milestones.text: Matiyasevich completes the proof that no algorithm decides whether a polynomial equation has integer solutions.

milestones.title: Machine-checked mathematics
milestones.text: Gonthier and Werner complete a fully computer-verified proof of the four colour theorem in the Coq proof assistant.

openQuestions.title: The 1/3–2/3 conjecture
openQuestions.q: In every finite partial order that is not a total order, are there two elements x and y such that x comes before y in between a third and two thirds of all compatible total orders?
openQuestions.known: Posed by Kislitsyn (1968) and independently by Fredman and Linial. Kahn and Saks (1984) proved a version with 3/11 in place of 1/3, Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter (1995) improved the constant to about 0.276, and the conjecture is known for many special classes of posets.

openQuestions.title: Frankl’s union-closed sets conjecture
openQuestions.q: If a finite family of sets is closed under unions, must some element belong to at least half of the sets?
openQuestions.known: Frankl posed it in 1979. Gilmer (2022) proved that some element lies in at least 1% of the sets, and follow-up work quickly raised this to about 38%, but one half remains unproved.

openQuestions.title: Finite lattice representation problem
openQuestions.q: Is every finite lattice the lattice of congruences of some finite algebra?
openQuestions.known: Pálfy and Pudlák (1980) showed this is equivalent to asking whether every finite lattice is an interval in the subgroup lattice of a finite group. Many small lattices are known to be representable, but the general question is open.

openQuestions.title: Rota’s basis conjecture
openQuestions.q: Given n bases of an n-dimensional vector space, can the vectors always be arranged in an n×n grid so that every row and every column is a basis?
openQuestions.known: Rota posed it in 1989. It is known for some small dimensions and in asymptotic forms (Pokrovskiy, 2020, and later improvements), but the full conjecture is open.

openQuestions.title: The sunflower conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is there a constant C such that any family of more than Cᵏ sets of size k contains three sets whose pairwise intersections are all the same?
openQuestions.known: Erdős and Rado (1960) proved a bound growing like k!. Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang (2019) improved it dramatically to about (log k)ᵏ, but an exponential bound Cᵏ remains open.

openQuestions.title: The Stanley–Stembridge conjecture
openQuestions.q: Are the chromatic symmetric functions of incomparability graphs of (3+1)-free posets always positive combinations of elementary symmetric functions?
openQuestions.known: Stanley and Stembridge proposed it in 1993, linking poset structure to symmetric functions. Many special cases were proved over thirty years, and Hikita posted a proof in 2024 that is being checked by the community.

milestones.title: An algebra of logic
milestones.text: Boole treats logical reasoning as algebra, the origin of Boolean algebras.

milestones.title: Lattices appear
milestones.text: Dedekind studies structures with meet and join, now called lattices.

milestones.title: Sperner’s theorem
milestones.text: Sperner finds the largest family of subsets in which no set contains another.

milestones.title: Distributive lattices as sets
milestones.text: Birkhoff shows every finite distributive lattice is a lattice of down-sets of a poset.

milestones.title: Dilworth’s theorem
milestones.text: Dilworth proves the largest antichain equals the fewest chains needed to cover a finite poset.

milestones.title: Fixed points in lattices
milestones.text: Tarski proves every order-preserving map on a complete lattice has a fixed point.

milestones.title: Möbius functions of posets
milestones.text: Rota develops Möbius inversion on posets, unifying many counting arguments.

discrete.name: Counting & graphs
discrete.label: arXiv math.CO · Combinatorics (MSC 05)
discrete.field: combinatorics and graph theory: enumeration, extremal and probabilistic combinatorics, Ramsey theory, graph structure and colouring
discrete.peopleNote: Six combinatorialists whose results on graphs, Ramsey theory and probabilistic methods shape the field and who still publish on arXiv.

openQuestions.title: Hadwiger’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: If a graph has no complete graph on t vertices as a minor, can it always be coloured with t − 1 colours?
openQuestions.known: Hadwiger posed it in 1943. It is proved for t ≤ 6, the case t = 6 by Robertson, Seymour and Thomas (1993), and is open for every larger t.

openQuestions.title: Diagonal Ramsey numbers
openQuestions.q: What is the smallest number of people guaranteeing five mutual friends or five mutual strangers, and how fast do these Ramsey numbers grow?
openQuestions.known: It is known that 43 ≤ R(5,5) ≤ 46, the upper bound by Angeltveit and McKay (2024). Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe (2023) made the first exponential improvement on the classical upper bound for R(k,k).

openQuestions.title: The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture
openQuestions.q: If a graph avoids some fixed induced subgraph, must it contain a clique or an independent set of polynomial size?
openQuestions.known: Erdős and Hajnal posed it in 1989. It is proved for several small forbidden graphs, including the five-vertex path (Nguyen, Scott and Seymour, 2023), but is open in general.

openQuestions.title: The reconstruction conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is every graph with at least three vertices determined by the collection of graphs obtained by deleting one vertex at a time?
openQuestions.known: Kelly and Ulam formulated it in the 1940s. It is known for trees, regular graphs and disconnected graphs, and has been checked by computer for small graphs, but no general proof exists.

openQuestions.title: The graceful tree conjecture
openQuestions.q: Can the vertices of every tree with n edges be labelled 0 to n so that the edge differences are exactly 1 to n?
openQuestions.known: Ringel and Kotzig posed it in the 1960s. The related Ringel conjecture on tree decompositions was proved in 2020 by Montgomery, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov, but graceful labelling of all trees remains open.

openQuestions.title: The cycle double cover conjecture
openQuestions.q: Does every graph without a bridge have a collection of cycles that covers every edge exactly twice?
openQuestions.known: Proposed by Szekeres (1973) and Seymour (1979). A minimal counterexample would have to be a snark, a special kind of cubic graph, but none is known.

milestones.title: The bridges of Königsberg
milestones.text: Euler proves no walk crosses each of the city’s seven bridges exactly once, founding graph theory.

milestones.title: The four colour problem
milestones.text: Francis Guthrie asks whether four colours suffice for every map.

milestones.title: Ramsey’s theorem
milestones.text: Ramsey shows complete disorder is impossible: large structures always contain ordered substructures.

milestones.title: The probabilistic method
milestones.text: Erdős uses random colourings to prove lower bounds for Ramsey numbers.

milestones.title: Random graphs
milestones.text: Erdős and Rényi begin the theory of random graphs and their sudden phase changes.

milestones.title: Szemerédi’s theorem
milestones.text: Szemerédi proves every dense set of integers contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.

milestones.title: Four colours suffice
milestones.text: Appel and Haken prove the four colour theorem with extensive computer checking.

milestones.title: Graph minors
milestones.text: Robertson and Seymour complete their proof that every minor-closed graph family has finitely many forbidden minors.

number.name: Number theory
number.label: arXiv math.NT · Number theory (MSC 11)
number.field: number theory: primes, Diophantine equations, L-functions, modular forms, arithmetic geometry and analytic methods
number.peopleNote: Six number theorists behind major recent advances on primes, L-functions and arithmetic geometry who still publish on arXiv.

openQuestions.title: The Riemann hypothesis
openQuestions.q: Do all non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie on the line with real part 1/2?
openQuestions.known: Riemann stated it in 1859. Over 40% of the zeros are known to lie on the line (Conrey, 1989, with later improvements) and trillions have been checked numerically, but the hypothesis, which controls the error in counting primes, is unproved.

openQuestions.title: The twin prime conjecture
openQuestions.q: Are there infinitely many pairs of primes that differ by 2?
openQuestions.known: Zhang (2013) proved infinitely many prime pairs differ by at most 70 million; Maynard and the Polymath project lowered the bound to 246. Reaching 2 seems to need new ideas.

openQuestions.title: Goldbach’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is every even number greater than 2 the sum of two primes?
openQuestions.known: Goldbach posed it in 1742. Helfgott (2013) proved the weak version that every odd number above 5 is a sum of three primes; the even case is verified by computer far beyond 10¹⁸ but unproved.

openQuestions.title: The abc conjecture
openQuestions.q: When a + b = c for coprime positive integers, is c almost always smaller than a fixed power, slightly above 1, of the product of the distinct primes dividing abc?
openQuestions.known: Masser and Oesterlé formulated it in 1985. Mochizuki released a claimed proof in 2012; Scholze and Stix (2018) identified what they consider a serious gap, and the claim is not accepted by most experts.

openQuestions.title: The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture
openQuestions.q: Does the order of vanishing of an elliptic curve’s L-function at s = 1 equal the number of independent rational points of infinite order?
openQuestions.known: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer proposed it from computer experiments in the 1960s. It is proved when that order is 0 or 1, by Gross and Zagier (1986) together with Kolyvagin (1989), but open in general.

openQuestions.title: The Collatz conjecture
openQuestions.q: If you repeatedly halve even numbers and send odd n to 3n + 1, do you always reach 1?
openQuestions.known: Collatz posed it in 1937. It is verified for enormous ranges of starting values, and Tao (2019) proved that almost all orbits attain almost bounded values, but no proof is known.

milestones.title: Infinitely many primes
milestones.text: Euclid proves there is no largest prime number.

milestones.title: Fermat’s little theorem
milestones.text: Fermat states that aᵖ − a is divisible by p for every prime p.

milestones.title: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
milestones.text: Gauss systematises modular arithmetic and proves quadratic reciprocity.

milestones.title: The zeta function and primes
milestones.text: Riemann links the distribution of primes to the zeros of the zeta function.

milestones.title: The prime number theorem
milestones.text: Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin prove there are about x / log x primes up to x.

milestones.title: Fermat’s Last Theorem
milestones.text: Wiles, with Taylor, completes the proof that xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ has no positive solutions for n > 2.

milestones.title: Primes in progression
milestones.text: Green and Tao prove the primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.

milestones.title: Bounded prime gaps
milestones.text: Zhang proves infinitely many pairs of primes lie within a fixed distance of each other.

geometry.name: Geometry
geometry.label: arXiv math.MG · Metric, convex & discrete geometry (MSC 51, 52)
geometry.field: geometry: metric, convex and discrete geometry, polytopes, packings and incidence problems
geometry.peopleNote: Six geometers known for landmark results on packings, polytopes and discrete geometry who still publish on arXiv.

openQuestions.title: The Hadwiger–Nelson problem
openQuestions.q: How many colours are needed to colour the plane so that no two points exactly one unit apart share a colour?
openQuestions.known: The answer is known to be 5, 6 or 7. The lower bound of 5 was found by de Grey in 2018 with computer help; the upper bound of 7 comes from a simple hexagon colouring.

openQuestions.title: The polynomial Hirsch conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is the diameter of the graph of every polytope bounded by a polynomial in its dimension and number of facets?
openQuestions.known: The original Hirsch conjecture was disproved by Santos (2010). The best general upper bound, due to Kalai and Kleitman (1992), is quasi-polynomial, so whether a polynomial bound holds, which matters for the simplex method, is open.

openQuestions.title: Kalai’s 3ᵈ conjecture
openQuestions.q: Does every centrally symmetric d-dimensional polytope have at least 3ᵈ non-empty faces in total?
openQuestions.known: Kalai proposed it in 1989; the cube attains the bound. It is proved in dimensions up to 4 (Sanyal, Werner and Ziegler, 2009) and for some special classes, but open in general.

openQuestions.title: The Erdős–Szekeres conjecture
openQuestions.q: Do 2ⁿ⁻² + 1 points in the plane, no three on a line, always contain n points forming a convex polygon?
openQuestions.known: Erdős and Szekeres conjectured this in 1935 and showed the number is finite. Suk (2017) proved 2ⁿ⁺ᵒ⁽ⁿ⁾ points suffice, matching the conjecture asymptotically; the exact value is known only for n ≤ 6.

openQuestions.title: The Erdős unit distance problem
openQuestions.q: How many pairs of points at distance exactly one can n points in the plane determine?
openQuestions.known: Erdős (1946) showed a grid gives slightly more than linearly many. The best upper bound, of order n^(4/3), dates from Spencer, Szemerédi and Trotter (1984), and closing the gap is open.

openQuestions.title: Kissing numbers
openQuestions.q: How many equal spheres can touch a central sphere of the same size in dimensions 5, 6 and 7?
openQuestions.known: Exact answers are known only in dimensions 1, 2, 3, 4, 8 and 24; dimension 4 was settled by Musin (2003). In dimension 5 the answer is known to lie between 40 and 44.

milestones.title: Euclid’s Elements
milestones.text: Euclid derives plane geometry from a short list of axioms and postulates.

milestones.title: Non-Euclidean geometry
milestones.text: Lobachevsky and Bolyai independently describe a consistent geometry in which the parallel postulate fails.

milestones.title: Riemannian geometry
milestones.text: Riemann’s lecture defines geometry intrinsically through a way of measuring lengths.

milestones.title: The Erlangen programme
milestones.text: Klein classifies geometries by the groups of transformations that preserve them.

milestones.title: Rigorous axioms
milestones.text: Hilbert gives a complete modern axiom system for Euclidean geometry.

milestones.title: The Kepler conjecture
milestones.text: Hales announces a computer-assisted proof that the familiar cannonball stacking is the densest sphere packing.

milestones.title: Packings in 8 and 24 dimensions
milestones.text: Viazovska proves the E8 lattice packing is densest in dimension 8, and with collaborators the Leech lattice in dimension 24.

openQuestions.title: The Hadamard conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is there a square matrix of ±1 entries with mutually orthogonal rows in every size that is a multiple of 4?
openQuestions.known: Paley (1933) conjectured this after constructing many such matrices. Constructions now cover most multiples of 4, but the smallest unresolved size is 668.

openQuestions.title: The exponent of matrix multiplication
openQuestions.q: Can two n × n matrices be multiplied using about n² arithmetic operations?
openQuestions.known: Strassen (1969) showed fewer than n³ operations suffice. Successive improvements brought the exponent ω below 2.372 by 2024, but whether ω = 2 is open.

openQuestions.title: Crouzeix’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: For any square matrix and polynomial, is the norm of p(A) at most twice the largest value of |p| on the numerical range of A?
openQuestions.known: Crouzeix proposed the constant 2 in 2004. Crouzeix and Palencia (2017) proved the bound with constant 1 + √2; the conjectured value 2 is open.

openQuestions.title: Permanent versus determinant
openQuestions.q: Can the permanent of an n × n matrix be written as the determinant of a matrix only polynomially larger?
openQuestions.known: Valiant (1979) showed this is an algebraic analogue of P versus NP. The best lower bound, of order n²/2, is due to Mignon and Ressayre (2004), far from the exponential size expected.

openQuestions.title: Mutually unbiased bases in dimension 6
openQuestions.q: In six-dimensional complex space, how many orthonormal bases can be chosen so that every pair is mutually unbiased?
openQuestions.known: In prime-power dimensions d there are d + 1 such bases (Wootters and Fields, 1989). In dimension 6 only 3 are known, and numerical evidence suggests no more exist, but no proof is known.

openQuestions.title: Zauner’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: Does every dimension d admit d² equiangular lines in complex d-dimensional space, giving a symmetric informationally complete measurement?
openQuestions.known: Zauner conjectured it in 1999. Exact or numerical solutions are known in many dimensions, with deep links to algebraic number theory, but no general construction is proved.

milestones.title: Determinants
milestones.text: Leibniz uses determinant-like expressions to solve systems of linear equations.

milestones.title: Cramer’s rule
milestones.text: Cramer publishes a formula solving linear systems with determinants.

milestones.title: Vector spaces in embryo
milestones.text: Grassmann’s Ausdehnungslehre describes linear combinations and dimension abstractly.

milestones.title: Matrix algebra
milestones.text: Cayley treats matrices as objects that can be added and multiplied.

milestones.title: Axioms for vector spaces
milestones.text: Peano gives the first axiomatic definition of a vector space.

milestones.title: Computing the SVD
milestones.text: Golub and Kahan introduce a practical algorithm for the singular value decomposition.

milestones.title: Faster multiplication
milestones.text: Strassen multiplies matrices with fewer than n³ operations.

milestones.title: Kadison–Singer resolved
milestones.text: Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava use interlacing polynomials to solve the Kadison–Singer problem.

groups.name: Groups & symmetry
groups.label: arXiv math.GR · Group theory (MSC 20)
groups.field: group theory: finite groups, geometric and combinatorial group theory, growth, representations and symmetry
groups.peopleNote: Six group theorists spanning finite, geometric and asymptotic group theory who still publish on arXiv.

openQuestions.title: The Burnside problem for B(2,5)
openQuestions.q: Is the largest group generated by two elements in which every element satisfies x⁵ = 1 finite?
openQuestions.known: Burnside asked such questions in 1902. Novikov and Adian (1968) showed the free Burnside groups are infinite for large odd exponents, and the cases of exponent 2, 3, 4 and 6 are finite, but exponent 5 is unresolved.

openQuestions.title: Kaplansky’s zero-divisor conjecture
openQuestions.q: If a group has no elements of finite order, can the product of two non-zero elements of its group ring be zero?
openQuestions.known: Kaplansky raised it in the 1950s. The related unit conjecture was disproved by Gardam (2021), but the zero-divisor conjecture is open, though known for many classes such as orderable groups.

openQuestions.title: Are hyperbolic groups residually finite?
openQuestions.q: In every word-hyperbolic group, can each non-identity element be detected in some finite quotient?
openQuestions.known: Hyperbolic groups were introduced by Gromov (1987). Agol (2013) and Wise proved residual finiteness for cubulated hyperbolic groups, but the general case is a central open question.

openQuestions.title: Whitehead’s asphericity conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is every connected subcomplex of a two-dimensional aspherical complex itself aspherical?
openQuestions.known: Whitehead posed it in 1941. Bestvina and Brady (1997) showed that a counterexample would also disprove either it or the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture, but the question is open.

openQuestions.title: The Andrews–Curtis conjecture
openQuestions.q: Can every balanced presentation of the trivial group be reduced to the trivial presentation using a standard list of moves?
openQuestions.known: Andrews and Curtis proposed it in 1965. Many potential counterexamples are known, and it is linked to the smooth Poincaré conjecture in dimension 4, but none has been resolved either way.

openQuestions.title: Are all groups sofic?
openQuestions.q: Can every group be approximated, in a precise statistical sense, by permutation groups of finite sets?
openQuestions.known: Gromov (1999) introduced the idea, and Weiss named it. Many conjectures, such as Gottschalk’s surjunctivity conjecture, are known for sofic groups, yet no non-sofic group has been found.

milestones.title: Galois groups
milestones.text: Galois links solvability of polynomial equations to groups of permutations of their roots.

milestones.title: Abstract groups
milestones.text: Cayley defines a group abstractly by its multiplication table.

milestones.title: Sylow theorems
milestones.text: Sylow proves the existence of subgroups of prime-power order in finite groups.

milestones.title: Dehn’s problems
milestones.text: Dehn poses the word, conjugacy and isomorphism problems for groups.

milestones.title: Undecidable word problem
milestones.text: Novikov, and Boone independently, construct groups with undecidable word problem.

milestones.title: Odd order theorem
milestones.text: Feit and Thompson prove every finite group of odd order is solvable.

milestones.title: Polynomial growth
milestones.text: Gromov proves groups of polynomial growth are virtually nilpotent.

milestones.title: Finite simple groups classified
milestones.text: Aschbacher and Smith’s work on quasithin groups completes the classification of finite simple groups.

rings.name: Rings, fields & polynomials
rings.label: arXiv math.AC · Commutative & noncommutative algebra (MSC 12, 13, 16)
rings.field: ring theory and field theory: commutative algebra, noncommutative rings, polynomial equations, Galois theory and homological methods
rings.peopleNote: Six algebraists central to commutative and computational algebra who still publish on arXiv.

openQuestions.title: The Jacobian conjecture
openQuestions.q: If a polynomial map from ℂⁿ to itself has a Jacobian determinant that is a non-zero constant, must it have a polynomial inverse?
openQuestions.known: Keller posed it in 1939. It is known in dimension 2 for polynomials of low degree and in many special cases, and many published proofs have turned out to be flawed.

openQuestions.title: The inverse Galois problem
openQuestions.q: Does every finite group arise as the Galois group of some extension of the rational numbers?
openQuestions.known: Hilbert (1892) showed symmetric and alternating groups occur, and Shafarevich (1954) proved it for all solvable groups. It is also known for 25 of the 26 sporadic simple groups, but open in general.

openQuestions.title: Hilbert’s twelfth problem
openQuestions.q: Can all abelian extensions of an arbitrary number field be generated explicitly by special values of analytic functions, as roots of unity do for the rationals?
openQuestions.known: The Kronecker–Weber theorem settles the rationals and complex multiplication settles imaginary quadratic fields. Dasgupta and Kakde (2021) gave an explicit answer for totally real fields using p-adic methods; general fields remain open.

openQuestions.title: The Dixmier conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is every endomorphism of the first Weyl algebra over a field of characteristic zero an automorphism?
openQuestions.known: Dixmier posed it in 1968. Tsuchimoto (2005) and Belov-Kanel and Kontsevich (2007) showed it is stably equivalent to the Jacobian conjecture.

openQuestions.title: Serre’s positivity conjecture
openQuestions.q: For two modules intersecting properly over a regular local ring, is Serre’s intersection multiplicity always positive?
openQuestions.known: Serre (1958) proved it in the unramified case. Roberts and Gillet–Soulé (1985) proved the vanishing conjecture and Gabber (1990s) proved non-negativity, but positivity in general is open.

openQuestions.title: The Casas-Alvero conjecture
openQuestions.q: If a complex polynomial of degree n shares a root with each of its first n − 1 derivatives, must it be (x − a)ⁿ?
openQuestions.known: Casas-Alvero proposed it around 2001. It is proved for degrees that are prime powers, or twice a prime power, by Graf von Bothmer, Labs, Schicho and van de Woestijne (2007) and Draisma and de Jong, but open in general.

milestones.title: The fundamental theorem of algebra
milestones.text: Gauss gives a proof that every non-constant polynomial has a complex root.

milestones.title: No quintic formula
milestones.text: Abel completes the proof that general quintic equations cannot be solved by radicals.

milestones.title: Galois theory
milestones.text: Galois characterises which polynomial equations are solvable by radicals.

milestones.title: Ideals
milestones.text: Dedekind introduces ideals to restore unique factorisation in rings of algebraic integers.

milestones.title: Hilbert’s basis theorem
milestones.text: Hilbert proves every ideal in a polynomial ring over a field is finitely generated.

milestones.title: Noetherian rings
milestones.text: Noether’s Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen founds modern abstract commutative algebra.

milestones.title: Gröbner bases
milestones.text: Buchberger gives an algorithm making polynomial ideal computations practical.

calculus.label: arXiv math.CA · Classical analysis (MSC 26)
calculus.field: classical analysis: real functions, inequalities, special functions, approximation and harmonic analysis
calculus.peopleNote: Six analysts whose work on classical and harmonic analysis is widely influential and who still publish on arXiv.

openQuestions.title: Is π + e irrational?
openQuestions.q: Is the sum of the two most famous constants of calculus an irrational number?
openQuestions.known: Both π (Lambert, 1761) and e (Euler, 1737) are irrational, and both are transcendental. It is known that at least one of π + e and πe is transcendental, but for neither number is irrationality proved.

openQuestions.title: Is Euler’s constant irrational?
openQuestions.q: Is the limit of 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n − log n, about 0.5772, an irrational number?
openQuestions.known: Euler introduced the constant in 1734. Its decimal expansion is computed to billions of digits, which shows any fraction equal to it would need an enormous denominator, but irrationality is unproved.

openQuestions.title: Schanuel’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: If complex numbers z₁, …, zₙ are linearly independent over the rationals, do zᵢ and e^(zᵢ) together contain at least n algebraically independent numbers?
openQuestions.known: Schanuel formulated it in the 1960s. It would imply the transcendence of e + π and many similar facts, but only special cases such as the Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem are known.

openQuestions.title: Irrationality of ζ(5)
openQuestions.q: Is 1 + 1/2⁵ + 1/3⁵ + … an irrational number?
openQuestions.known: Apéry (1978) proved ζ(3) is irrational. Ball and Rivoal (2001) showed infinitely many odd zeta values are irrational and Zudilin (2001) that one of ζ(5), ζ(7), ζ(9), ζ(11) is, but no single one beyond ζ(3) is known.

openQuestions.title: Is Catalan’s constant irrational?
openQuestions.q: Is 1 − 1/3² + 1/5² − 1/7² + …, about 0.9160, an irrational number?
openQuestions.known: The constant appears throughout combinatorics and analysis and is computed to billions of digits, yet whether it is irrational, let alone transcendental, is unknown.

openQuestions.title: The Pompeiu problem
openQuestions.q: If a bounded smooth region has the property that a continuous function integrating to zero over every rigid motion of it must vanish, does that fail only for discs?
openQuestions.known: Pompeiu raised the question in 1929. Discs are known to fail the property, and Williams (1976) linked counterexamples to Schiffer’s overdetermined problem, but the general case is open.

milestones.title: Fluxions
milestones.text: Newton develops his method of fluxions for rates of change and areas.

milestones.title: Calculus in print
milestones.text: Leibniz publishes the differential calculus with the dx notation still used today.

milestones.title: The Analyst
milestones.text: Berkeley criticises infinitesimals as “ghosts of departed quantities”.

milestones.title: Rigorous limits
milestones.text: Cauchy’s Cours d’analyse bases calculus on limits and continuity.

milestones.title: The Riemann integral
milestones.text: Riemann gives a precise definition of the integral via sums over partitions.

milestones.title: A pathological function
milestones.text: Weierstrass presents a function that is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere.

milestones.title: Infinitesimals made rigorous
milestones.text: Robinson’s non-standard analysis gives infinitesimals a sound logical foundation.

analysis.label: arXiv math.CA · Real analysis, series & approximation (MSC 26, 40, 41)

analysis.field: real analysis: series, convergence, Fourier analysis, approximation and geometric harmonic analysis
analysis.peopleNote: Six analysts behind recent advances in Fourier analysis, approximation and additive problems who still publish on arXiv.

openQuestions.title: The Kakeya conjecture
openQuestions.q: Must a set in n-dimensional space that contains a unit line segment in every direction have full dimension n?
openQuestions.known: Davies (1971) proved it in the plane, and Wang and Zahl (2025) proved it in three dimensions. Dimensions four and higher remain open.

openQuestions.title: The Bochner–Riesz conjecture
openQuestions.q: For which exponents do Bochner–Riesz means of Fourier series and integrals converge in Lᵖ?
openQuestions.known: Carleson and Sjölin (1972) settled the plane. In three and more dimensions only partial ranges are known, with recent progress from polynomial partitioning (Guth, Hickman and Iliopoulou, 2019).

openQuestions.title: The Littlewood conjecture
openQuestions.q: For any two real numbers α and β, does n·‖nα‖·‖nβ‖ get arbitrarily close to zero?
openQuestions.known: Littlewood posed it around 1930. Einsiedler, Katok and Lindenstrauss (2006) proved the possible exceptions form a set of Hausdorff dimension zero.

openQuestions.title: Erdős’s conjecture on arithmetic progressions
openQuestions.q: If the sum of the reciprocals of a set of positive integers diverges, must the set contain arithmetic progressions of every length?
openQuestions.known: Erdős posed it in 1936 (with Turán) and offered a large prize. Bloom and Sisask (2020) proved it for three-term progressions; longer progressions remain open.

openQuestions.title: The Flint Hills series
openQuestions.q: Does the series 1/(n³ sin² n), summed over all positive integers n, converge?
openQuestions.known: Pickover popularised it in 2002. Its convergence is tied to how well π can be approximated by fractions: Alekseyev (2011) showed it would converge if π’s irrationality measure were below 2.5.

openQuestions.title: The lonely runner conjecture
openQuestions.q: If k runners with distinct constant speeds circle a unit track, is every runner at some time at least 1/k away from all others?
openQuestions.known: Wills (1967) and Cusick (1973) posed equivalent forms. It is proved for small numbers of runners, up to seven by Barajas and Serra (2008), but open in general.

milestones.title: The harmonic series diverges
milestones.text: Oresme proves 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … grows without bound.

milestones.title: The Basel problem
milestones.text: Euler shows 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + … equals π²/6.

milestones.title: Fourier series
milestones.text: Fourier claims any function can be written as a sum of sines and cosines.

milestones.title: Constructing the reals
milestones.text: Dedekind defines real numbers by cuts of the rationals.

milestones.title: Polynomial approximation
milestones.text: Weierstrass proves every continuous function on an interval is a uniform limit of polynomials.

milestones.title: Carleson’s theorem
milestones.text: Carleson proves the Fourier series of a square-integrable function converges almost everywhere.

openQuestions.title: The smooth four-dimensional Poincaré conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is every smooth four-dimensional manifold that is a homotopy sphere actually the standard smooth four-sphere?
openQuestions.known: Freedman (1982) proved the topological version, and the analogue holds in every other dimension. In dimension 4 smooth structures behave unusually, and the question is open.

openQuestions.title: The unknotting problem
openQuestions.q: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm to decide whether a knot diagram represents the unknot?
openQuestions.known: Haken (1961) gave the first algorithm. The problem is in NP (Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger, 1999) and in co-NP (Lackenby), and Lackenby announced a quasi-polynomial algorithm in 2021, but polynomial time is open.

openQuestions.title: The slice–ribbon conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is every slice knot a ribbon knot?
openQuestions.known: Fox posed it in 1962. It is known for two-bridge knots (Lisca, 2007) and some other families, but open in general.

openQuestions.title: The volume conjecture
openQuestions.q: Do the coloured Jones polynomials of a hyperbolic knot determine the volume of its complement through their growth rate?
openQuestions.known: Kashaev (1997) and H. and J. Murakami (2001) formulated it. It is checked for several knots, including the figure-eight knot, but unproved in general.

openQuestions.title: The Hilbert–Smith conjecture
openQuestions.q: Can a compact group that acts faithfully on a manifold fail to be a Lie group?
openQuestions.known: The conjecture says no. It is equivalent to ruling out faithful actions of the p-adic integers, and Pardon (2013) proved it for three-manifolds, but higher dimensions are open.

openQuestions.title: The Borel conjecture
openQuestions.q: Are closed aspherical manifolds with isomorphic fundamental groups always homeomorphic?
openQuestions.known: Borel raised it in 1953. It is known for many groups, including hyperbolic and CAT(0) groups in high dimensions (Bartels and Lück, 2012), but open in general.

milestones.title: Euler’s polyhedron formula
milestones.text: Euler observes that vertices − edges + faces = 2 for convex polyhedra.

milestones.title: One-sided surfaces
milestones.text: Möbius and Listing describe a surface with only one side.

milestones.title: Analysis Situs
milestones.text: Poincaré introduces homology and the fundamental group.

milestones.title: Topological spaces
milestones.text: Hausdorff gives an axiomatic definition of topological space.

milestones.title: High-dimensional Poincaré
milestones.text: Smale proves the Poincaré conjecture in dimensions five and above.

milestones.title: Dimension four
milestones.text: Freedman proves the topological four-dimensional Poincaré conjecture.

milestones.title: The Jones polynomial
milestones.text: Jones discovers a new knot invariant from operator algebras.

milestones.title: Geometrisation
milestones.text: Perelman proves Thurston’s geometrisation conjecture, including the Poincaré conjecture.

milestones.title: Virtual Haken
milestones.text: Agol proves every closed hyperbolic three-manifold has a finite cover containing an embedded incompressible surface.

complex.peopleNote: Six complex analysts, including leaders in complex dynamics and function theory, who still publish on arXiv.

openQuestions.title: Is the Mandelbrot set locally connected?
openQuestions.q: Is the Mandelbrot set locally connected, which would give a complete picture of quadratic dynamics?
openQuestions.known: Douady and Hubbard (1980s) showed it is connected. Yoccoz proved local connectivity at many points, Lyubich extended this, and the full conjecture would imply density of hyperbolic parameters.

openQuestions.title: The Lindelöf hypothesis
openQuestions.q: Does the Riemann zeta function grow more slowly than any positive power of t along the critical line?
openQuestions.known: Lindelöf conjectured it in 1908; it follows from the Riemann hypothesis. Bourgain (2017) proved growth at most t to the power 13/84 + ε, still far from the conjecture.

openQuestions.title: Bloch’s constant
openQuestions.q: What is the largest radius of a disc that the image of every normalised holomorphic map of the unit disc must contain injectively?
openQuestions.known: Bloch (1925) showed such a constant exists. Ahlfors and Grunsky (1937) conjectured an exact value of about 0.4719; the best proved lower bound is still below it.

openQuestions.title: Does the Mandelbrot set’s boundary have positive area?
openQuestions.q: Is the boundary of the Mandelbrot set so wiggly that it occupies positive area in the plane?
openQuestions.known: Shishikura (1998) proved the boundary has Hausdorff dimension 2, the largest possible. Whether it has positive area is open, and a positive answer would have striking consequences for quadratic dynamics.

openQuestions.title: The corona problem in several variables
openQuestions.q: In the unit ball of ℂⁿ, n ≥ 2, is the open ball dense in the maximal ideal space of bounded holomorphic functions?
openQuestions.known: Carleson (1962) proved the corona theorem for the unit disc. In higher dimensions the question is open for the ball and the polydisc.

openQuestions.title: Eremenko’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: For a transcendental entire function, is every connected component of the set of escaping points unbounded?
openQuestions.known: Eremenko (1989) showed the escaping set is non-empty and posed the question. Rottenfusser, Rückert, Rempe and Schleicher (2011) found a counterexample to a strong form, but the conjecture as stated is open.

milestones.title: Square roots of negatives
milestones.text: Cardano meets square roots of negative numbers while solving cubic equations.

milestones.title: Euler’s formula
milestones.text: Euler shows e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ.

milestones.title: The complex plane
milestones.text: Argand pictures complex numbers as points in a plane.

milestones.title: Cauchy’s integral theorem
milestones.text: Cauchy shows integrals of holomorphic functions around closed loops vanish.

milestones.title: Riemann’s thesis
milestones.text: Riemann introduces Riemann surfaces and states the mapping theorem.

milestones.title: Iterating maps
milestones.text: Julia and Fatou study iterating rational functions, founding complex dynamics.

milestones.title: The Mandelbrot set
milestones.text: Computer images of the Mandelbrot set reveal its intricate structure.

milestones.title: Bieberbach conjecture
milestones.text: De Branges proves the coefficient bound for univalent functions.

measure.label: arXiv math.CA · Measure & geometric measure theory (MSC 28)

openQuestions.title: Falconer’s distance problem
openQuestions.q: If a planar set has Hausdorff dimension above 1, must its set of pairwise distances have positive length?
openQuestions.known: Falconer (1985) showed dimension above 3/2 suffices. Guth, Iosevich, Ou and Wang (2020) lowered this to 5/4, but the conjectured threshold of 1 is open.

openQuestions.title: The inscribed square problem
openQuestions.q: Does every simple closed curve in the plane pass through the four corners of some square?
openQuestions.known: Toeplitz posed it in 1911. It is proved for convex and for smooth curves, and Greene and Lobb (2020) showed smooth curves contain rectangles of every aspect ratio, but for arbitrary continuous curves the question is open.

openQuestions.title: Mahler’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: Among centrally symmetric convex bodies, is the product of the volume and the volume of its polar body smallest for the cube?
openQuestions.known: Mahler posed it in 1939 and proved the plane case. Iriyeh and Shibata (2020) proved dimension three; dimension four and above are open.

openQuestions.title: Lebesgue’s universal covering problem
openQuestions.q: What is the smallest area of a convex shape that can cover every planar set of diameter 1?
openQuestions.known: Lebesgue posed it in 1914. Successive constructions have reduced the upper bound to about 0.8441 (Baez, Bagdasaryan and Gibbs, 2015), but the exact value is unknown.

openQuestions.title: Moser’s worm problem
openQuestions.q: What is the smallest area of a region that can be moved to cover every curve of length 1?
openQuestions.known: Moser posed it in 1966. Upper and lower bounds have been improved many times, but the exact minimum area, and even its shape, are unknown.

openQuestions.title: Heilbronn’s triangle problem
openQuestions.q: How large can the smallest triangle formed by n points in a unit square be made?
openQuestions.known: Heilbronn posed it around 1950. Komlós, Pintz and Szemerédi (1982) gave a lower bound of order log n / n², and recent work by Cohen, Pohoata and Zakharov (2023) improved the upper bound, but the true order is open.

milestones.title: The Cantor set
milestones.text: Cantor describes an uncountable set of total length zero.

milestones.title: Borel sets
milestones.text: Borel defines measurable sets built from intervals by countable operations.

milestones.title: The Lebesgue integral
milestones.text: Lebesgue’s thesis defines integration through measure, handling far more functions than Riemann’s.

milestones.title: A non-measurable set
milestones.text: Vitali constructs a set of reals with no sensible length, using the axiom of choice.

milestones.title: Hausdorff dimension
milestones.text: Hausdorff defines a notion of dimension that can take fractional values.

milestones.title: Banach–Tarski
milestones.text: Banach and Tarski show a ball can be cut into finitely many pieces and reassembled into two balls.

milestones.title: Radon–Nikodym
milestones.text: Nikodym proves densities exist between absolutely continuous measures in full generality.

milestones.title: Integral currents
milestones.text: Federer and Fleming introduce currents, transforming the study of minimal surfaces.

probability.name: Probability & stochastic processes
probability.label: arXiv math.PR · Probability (MSC 60)
probability.field: probability theory: random walks, percolation, random geometry, stochastic PDE, random matrices and statistical physics models
probability.peopleNote: Six probabilists behind major advances in percolation, random geometry and stochastic PDE who still publish on arXiv.

openQuestions.title: Critical percolation in three dimensions
openQuestions.q: In bond percolation on the three-dimensional cubic lattice at the critical density, is there almost surely no infinite cluster?
openQuestions.known: The answer is yes in two dimensions (Harris and Kesten, 1960 and 1980) and in high dimensions via the lace expansion (now dimension 11 and above, Fitzner and van der Hofstad, 2017). Dimensions 3 to 10 are open.

openQuestions.title: Self-avoiding walk in the plane
openQuestions.q: Does the uniform self-avoiding walk on a planar lattice converge, when rescaled, to the random curve SLE(8/3)?
openQuestions.known: Lawler, Schramm and Werner (2002) conjectured this and showed it would follow from a suitable continuum limit. Duminil-Copin and Smirnov (2010) computed the connective constant of the hexagonal lattice, √(2 + √2).

openQuestions.title: Universality of critical percolation
openQuestions.q: Is critical percolation conformally invariant on the square lattice, as Smirnov proved for the triangular lattice?
openQuestions.known: Smirnov (2001) proved Cardy’s formula and conformal invariance for site percolation on the triangular lattice. Extending this to other planar lattices is a central open problem.

openQuestions.title: KPZ universality
openQuestions.q: Do all models of randomly growing interfaces in the KPZ class share the same large-scale fluctuations?
openQuestions.known: Kardar, Parisi and Zhang (1986) predicted universal behaviour. Exactly solvable models have been analysed in detail, and Matetski, Quastel and Remenik (2021) constructed the KPZ fixed point, but universality is unproved for general models.

openQuestions.title: Delocalisation in the Anderson model
openQuestions.q: In three dimensions with weak disorder, does the Anderson model have extended states, so electrons can still conduct?
openQuestions.known: Anderson (1958) predicted localisation for strong disorder, now proved. The existence of extended states for weak disorder in three dimensions, expected by physicists, has never been proved.

openQuestions.title: The cutoff phenomenon
openQuestions.q: Which Markov chains mix abruptly, staying far from equilibrium and then reaching it within a short window?
openQuestions.known: Aldous and Diaconis (1986) identified cutoff, for example in card shuffling. Peres conjectured a simple criterion for reversible chains, which is known to fail in general and holds for some classes, but a characterisation is open.

milestones.title: The problem of points
milestones.text: Pascal and Fermat correspond on dividing stakes in an unfinished game, founding probability theory.

milestones.title: The law of large numbers
milestones.text: Bernoulli’s Ars Conjectandi proves averages of repeated trials settle down.

milestones.title: The normal curve
milestones.text: De Moivre approximates binomial probabilities by the bell-shaped normal curve.

milestones.title: Markov chains
milestones.text: Markov studies sequences in which the next state depends only on the present.

milestones.title: Brownian motion
milestones.text: Wiener constructs Brownian motion as a rigorous random process.

milestones.title: Axioms for probability
milestones.text: Kolmogorov founds probability on measure theory.

milestones.title: Stochastic calculus
milestones.text: Itô defines integrals with respect to Brownian motion.

milestones.title: Schramm–Loewner evolution
milestones.text: Schramm introduces SLE, random curves describing critical planar models.

milestones.title: Regularity structures
milestones.text: Hairer develops a theory giving meaning to singular stochastic PDE.

equations.field: differential equations: existence, regularity and long-time behaviour of ODE and PDE, including fluids, waves and free boundaries
equations.peopleNote: Six analysts whose work on regularity, fluids and waves defines modern PDE and who still publish on arXiv.

openQuestions.title: Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness
openQuestions.q: Do smooth initial flows of an incompressible fluid in three dimensions always stay smooth for all time?
openQuestions.known: Leray (1934) constructed weak solutions that exist forever, but their uniqueness and smoothness are unknown. It is a Clay Millennium Problem. In September 2026 OpenAI proposed a solution to one of the official formulations, the variant with a smooth external force; the claim is not yet verified and is the subject of a priority controversy.

openQuestions.title: Blow-up for the Euler equations
openQuestions.q: Can a smooth, finite-energy solution of the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations, with no boundary, develop a singularity in finite time?
openQuestions.known: Elgindi (2021) proved blow-up for slightly less smooth data, and Chen and Hou (2022) gave a computer-assisted proof of blow-up in a domain with a boundary. The smooth case without boundary is open.

openQuestions.title: Hilbert’s sixteenth problem
openQuestions.q: Is there a bound, depending only on the degree, for the number of limit cycles of a planar polynomial vector field?
openQuestions.known: Hilbert posed it in 1900. Ilyashenko (1991) and Écalle (1992) proved each such field has finitely many limit cycles, but no uniform bound is known even for quadratic fields.

openQuestions.title: Calderón’s inverse problem
openQuestions.q: Can the electrical conductivity inside a body be determined uniquely from voltage and current measurements on its surface, for any bounded conductivity?
openQuestions.known: Calderón posed it in 1980. Sylvester and Uhlmann (1987) proved uniqueness for smooth conductivities in three dimensions and Astala and Päivärinta (2006) for all bounded conductivities in the plane; rough conductivities in three dimensions are open.

openQuestions.title: Hearing the shape of a convex drum
openQuestions.q: Do the vibration frequencies of a smooth convex drum determine its shape?
openQuestions.known: Kac asked the general question in 1966. Gordon, Webb and Wolpert (1992) built different polygons with the same frequencies, but for smooth convex drums the answer is unknown.

openQuestions.title: Yang–Mills existence and mass gap
openQuestions.q: Does quantum Yang–Mills theory on four-dimensional space exist rigorously, with a positive lowest energy above the vacuum?
openQuestions.known: Physicists use Yang–Mills theory to describe the strong force, and the mass gap is supported by experiment and simulation. A mathematical construction is a Clay Millennium Problem.

milestones.title: The wave equation
milestones.text: D’Alembert writes down and solves the equation of a vibrating string.

milestones.title: Fluid motion
milestones.text: Euler formulates the equations of motion of an ideal fluid.

milestones.title: The heat equation
milestones.text: Fourier publishes his analytical theory of heat and its equation.

milestones.title: Viscous fluids
milestones.text: Stokes completes the derivation of the Navier–Stokes equations.

milestones.title: Limit cycles
milestones.text: Bendixson completes the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem on long-term planar behaviour.

milestones.title: Weak solutions
milestones.text: Leray constructs global weak solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations.

milestones.title: Sobolev spaces
milestones.text: Sobolev introduces function spaces that underpin modern PDE theory.

dynamics.label: arXiv math.DS · Dynamical systems (MSC 37)
dynamics.field: dynamical systems and ergodic theory: chaos, stability, homogeneous dynamics, billiards and one-dimensional dynamics
dynamics.peopleNote: Six researchers whose work on ergodic theory, chaos and homogeneous dynamics shapes the field and who still publish on arXiv.

openQuestions.title: Furstenberg’s ×2 ×3 conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is Lebesgue measure the only non-atomic probability measure on the circle invariant under both doubling and tripling?
openQuestions.known: Furstenberg (1967) proved the analogous statement for closed invariant sets. Rudolph (1990) proved it for measures of positive entropy; the zero-entropy case is open.

openQuestions.title: Chaos in the standard map
openQuestions.q: For large parameter values, does the Chirikov standard map have positive Lyapunov exponent on a set of positive area?
openQuestions.known: Numerical experiments strongly suggest widespread chaos. Elliptic islands persist for many parameters, and proving positive metric entropy remains a famous open problem.

openQuestions.title: Arnold diffusion
openQuestions.q: In generic nearly integrable Hamiltonian systems with three or more degrees of freedom, can orbits drift a long way in action?
openQuestions.known: Arnold (1964) gave an example of such drift. Mather announced results for generic systems, and significant progress was made by Bernard, Kaloshin and Zhang and others, but the general conjecture is open.

openQuestions.title: Periodic billiards in triangles
openQuestions.q: Does every triangular billiard table have a periodic trajectory?
openQuestions.known: Fagnano’s orbit works for acute triangles, and Schwartz (2009) proved the answer is yes for triangles with all angles at most 100°. Obtuse triangles in general are open.

openQuestions.title: Rokhlin’s multiple mixing problem
openQuestions.q: Does every mixing measure-preserving transformation mix sets of all orders?
openQuestions.known: Rokhlin asked this in 1949. Kalikow (1984) proved it for rank-one transformations and Host (1991) for systems with singular spectrum, but it is open in general.

openQuestions.title: Density of hyperbolicity in complex dynamics
openQuestions.q: Can every complex quadratic polynomial be approximated by ones whose orbits settle onto attracting cycles?
openQuestions.known: For real polynomials this was proved by Lyubich and by Graczyk and Świątek (1997), and generally by Kozlovski, Shen and van Strien (2007). The complex case is open and is implied by local connectivity of the Mandelbrot set.

milestones.title: Chaos in the three-body problem
milestones.text: Poincaré discovers complicated orbits while studying the stability of the solar system.

milestones.title: The ergodic theorem
milestones.text: Birkhoff proves time averages equal space averages almost everywhere for measure-preserving systems.

milestones.title: KAM theory
milestones.text: Kolmogorov announces that most quasi-periodic motions survive small perturbations.

milestones.title: The Lorenz attractor
milestones.text: Lorenz finds sensitive dependence on initial conditions in a simple weather model.

milestones.title: The horseshoe
milestones.text: Smale’s survey makes hyperbolic dynamics, including his horseshoe map, a central theory.

milestones.title: Universality in period doubling
milestones.text: Feigenbaum discovers universal constants governing the route to chaos.

milestones.title: Lorenz attractor proved
milestones.text: Tucker gives a computer-assisted proof that the Lorenz attractor exists.

openQuestions.title: The Hopf conjecture on positive curvature
openQuestions.q: Can the product of two 2-spheres carry a metric of strictly positive sectional curvature?
openQuestions.known: Hopf asked this in the 1930s. Closed manifolds of positive curvature are rare: beyond spheres and projective spaces, only isolated examples in low dimensions are known (Berger, Wallach, Aloff–Wallach, Eschenburg, Bazaikin), and S²×S² remains undecided.

openQuestions.title: The sign of the Euler characteristic
openQuestions.q: Does every closed, non-positively curved manifold of dimension 2n have Euler characteristic of sign (−1)ⁿ or zero?
openQuestions.known: This is another conjecture attributed to Hopf (and to Chern and Thurston for aspherical manifolds). It holds in dimensions 2 and 4, where it follows from the Gauss–Bonnet–Chern formula, but is open in higher dimensions.

openQuestions.title: The smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is every smooth 4-manifold that is homotopy equivalent to the 4-sphere actually diffeomorphic to it?
openQuestions.known: The topological version was proved by Freedman (1982), and the analogues hold in every other dimension. Whether exotic smooth 4-spheres exist is one of the central open problems linking geometry and topology.

openQuestions.title: The Yau–Tian–Donaldson conjecture in general
openQuestions.q: Does a compact Kähler manifold admit a metric of constant scalar curvature in a given class exactly when it is K-stable?
openQuestions.known: For Fano manifolds and Kähler–Einstein metrics this was proved by Chen, Donaldson and Sun (2015). For general polarised manifolds, with constant scalar curvature metrics, the expected equivalence is still not fully established.

openQuestions.title: The Carathéodory conjecture
openQuestions.q: Must every smooth closed convex surface in space have at least two umbilic points, where it curves equally in all directions?
openQuestions.known: The conjecture goes back to Carathéodory in the 1920s and holds for real-analytic surfaces by work of Hamburger, Bol and Klotz, though those proofs were long debated. Guilfoyle and Klingenberg have claimed a proof for smooth surfaces that is not yet universally accepted.

openQuestions.title: A complex structure on the six-sphere
openQuestions.q: Can the 6-sphere be given the structure of a complex manifold?
openQuestions.known: The 6-sphere has an almost complex structure coming from the octonions, and it is known that no such structure is compatible with the round metric in the integrable way (LeBrun, 1987). Several claimed answers, including one by Atiyah (2016), have not been accepted.

milestones.title: Curvature is intrinsic
milestones.text: Gauss’s Theorema Egregium shows the curvature of a surface can be measured from within the surface itself.

milestones.title: Riemannian geometry
milestones.text: Riemann’s habilitation lecture introduces manifolds of any dimension with a notion of distance and curvature.

milestones.title: Geometry of gravity
milestones.text: Einstein’s general relativity describes gravitation as the curvature of a four-dimensional Lorentzian manifold.

milestones.title: An intrinsic Gauss–Bonnet theorem
milestones.text: Chern gives an intrinsic proof of the generalised Gauss–Bonnet theorem, linking curvature to the Euler characteristic.

milestones.title: Every manifold sits in Euclidean space
milestones.text: Nash proves every Riemannian manifold can be isometrically embedded in some Euclidean space.

milestones.title: The Calabi conjecture
milestones.text: Yau proves the Calabi conjecture, producing Ricci-flat Kähler metrics now known as Calabi–Yau metrics.

milestones.title: Ricci flow
milestones.text: Hamilton introduces the Ricci flow, which deforms a metric to smooth out its curvature.

milestones.title: Geometrisation
milestones.text: Perelman completes his Ricci-flow proof of Thurston’s geometrisation conjecture, including the Poincaré conjecture.

milestones.title: The Willmore conjecture
milestones.text: Marques and Neves prove the Willmore conjecture using min-max theory for minimal surfaces.

openQuestions.title: Homotopy groups of spheres
openQuestions.q: Is there a way to compute all the homotopy groups of spheres, or at least to understand their overall pattern?
openQuestions.known: Serre (1953) showed they are finite apart from a few exceptions, yet no general formula is known. Machine-assisted methods have pushed complete computations of the stable groups to dimension 90 (Isaksen, Wang and Xu, 2023).

openQuestions.title: The Novikov conjecture
openQuestions.q: Are the higher signatures of a closed manifold always invariant under homotopy equivalence?
openQuestions.known: Novikov posed the conjecture around 1970. It is proved for large classes of fundamental groups, including hyperbolic groups and groups that embed coarsely in Hilbert space (Yu, 2000), but remains open in general.

openQuestions.title: The Borel conjecture
openQuestions.q: Are two closed aspherical manifolds with isomorphic fundamental groups necessarily homeomorphic?
openQuestions.known: Borel raised the question in 1953. Farrell and Jones proved it for non-positively curved manifolds of dimension at least 5, and Bartels and Lück (2012) extended it to hyperbolic and CAT(0) groups, but the general case is open.

openQuestions.title: Whitehead’s asphericity conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is every connected subcomplex of an aspherical 2-dimensional complex itself aspherical?
openQuestions.known: J. H. C. Whitehead asked this in 1941. Bestvina and Brady (1997) showed that it and the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture cannot both be true, but which one fails is unknown.

openQuestions.title: The Andrews–Curtis conjecture
openQuestions.q: Can every balanced presentation of the trivial group be reduced to the trivial presentation by a standard set of moves?
openQuestions.known: Andrews and Curtis proposed it in 1965, with links to 4-dimensional topology. Several families of potential counterexamples have resisted all attempts at reduction, while some candidates have since been trivialised by computer search.

openQuestions.title: The Hilbert–Smith conjecture
openQuestions.q: Can a group of p-adic integers act faithfully and continuously on a manifold?
openQuestions.known: The conjecture says it cannot, which would characterise Lie groups among locally compact groups acting on manifolds. It is proved in dimensions up to 3 (Pardon, 2013) and for smooth or Lipschitz actions, but is open in general.

milestones.title: Analysis Situs
milestones.text: Poincaré’s Analysis Situs founds algebraic topology, introducing homology and the fundamental group.

milestones.title: The Hopf fibration
milestones.text: Hopf shows that the 3-sphere maps onto the 2-sphere in an essential way, revealing that higher homotopy groups of spheres can be non-trivial.

milestones.title: Axioms for homology
milestones.text: Eilenberg and Steenrod characterise homology theories by a short list of axioms.

milestones.title: Exotic spheres
milestones.text: Milnor discovers smooth structures on the 7-sphere that are not diffeomorphic to the standard one.

milestones.title: Hopf invariant one
milestones.text: Adams proves that maps of Hopf invariant one exist only in dimensions 1, 2, 4 and 8.

milestones.title: Four-dimensional topology
milestones.text: Freedman proves the topological 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture, while Donaldson’s work shows smooth 4-manifolds behave very differently.

milestones.title: The Kervaire invariant problem
milestones.text: Hill, Hopkins and Ravenel show that Kervaire invariant one manifolds cannot exist beyond dimension 126.

milestones.title: Non-triangulable manifolds
milestones.text: Manolescu shows that in every dimension from 5 upwards there are manifolds that admit no triangulation.

openQuestions.title: The Hodge conjecture
openQuestions.q: On a smooth complex projective variety, is every rational cohomology class of Hodge type (p,p) a combination of classes of algebraic subvarieties?
openQuestions.known: Hodge formulated it in the 1950 International Congress; it is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems. It is known for divisors (Lefschetz, 1924) and some special varieties, while the integral version is false (Atiyah and Hirzebruch, 1962).

openQuestions.title: Resolution of singularities in positive characteristic
openQuestions.q: Can every algebraic variety over a field of positive characteristic be replaced by a smooth one through birational changes?
openQuestions.known: Hironaka proved resolution in characteristic zero (1964). In positive characteristic it is known up to dimension three (Abhyankar for surfaces; Cossart and Piltant for threefolds, 2008–2009), but open in general.

openQuestions.title: The Jacobian conjecture
openQuestions.q: If a polynomial map from n-space to itself has constant non-zero Jacobian determinant, must it have a polynomial inverse?
openQuestions.known: Keller posed the question in 1939. It is open even for two variables, though it is known for low-degree maps, and many published proofs have turned out to be wrong.

openQuestions.title: The abundance conjecture
openQuestions.q: For a variety whose canonical class is nef, is some multiple of the canonical class free of base points?
openQuestions.known: Abundance is a key missing step in the minimal model program. It is known for varieties of dimension at most three (Miyaoka, Kawamata and others), but open in higher dimensions.

openQuestions.title: Grothendieck’s standard conjectures
openQuestions.q: Do algebraic cycles behave well enough to give a universal cohomology theory of motives?
openQuestions.known: Grothendieck proposed the standard conjectures in the 1960s as a route to the Weil conjectures. Deligne proved the Weil conjectures by other means (1974), but the standard conjectures remain largely open, especially in positive characteristic.

openQuestions.title: The Nagata conjecture
openQuestions.q: What is the smallest degree of a plane curve passing with given multiplicity through many general points?
openQuestions.known: Nagata (1959) conjectured a lower bound for at least ten general points and used the case of a square number of points in his counterexample to Hilbert’s fourteenth problem. Only the square case is known.

milestones.title: Riemann surfaces
milestones.text: Riemann’s dissertation introduces Riemann surfaces, making algebraic curves objects of geometry.

milestones.title: Hilbert’s basis theorem
milestones.text: Hilbert proves every ideal in a polynomial ring is finitely generated.

milestones.title: The Nullstellensatz
milestones.text: Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz links ideals of polynomials to the sets of points where they vanish.

milestones.title: Schemes
milestones.text: Grothendieck begins publishing EGA, rebuilding algebraic geometry on the language of schemes.

milestones.title: Resolving singularities
milestones.text: Hironaka proves every variety in characteristic zero can be resolved into a smooth one.

milestones.title: The Weil conjectures
milestones.text: Deligne completes the proof of the Weil conjectures, including the analogue of the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields.

milestones.title: Minimal models of threefolds
milestones.text: Mori proves the existence of flips for threefolds, completing the minimal model program in dimension three.

milestones.title: Finite generation
milestones.text: Birkar, Cascini, Hacon and McKernan prove finite generation of the canonical ring for varieties of general type.

openQuestions.title: The Kakeya conjecture in higher dimensions
openQuestions.q: Must a set containing a unit line segment in every direction in n-dimensional space have full dimension n?
openQuestions.known: Davies proved the plane case (1971). Wang and Zahl announced a proof for three dimensions in 2025; the conjecture is open in dimensions four and above.

openQuestions.title: The Fourier restriction conjecture
openQuestions.q: For which exponents can the Fourier transform of a function be meaningfully restricted to a curved surface such as a sphere?
openQuestions.known: Stein posed the problem in the 1960s; the plane case was settled by Fefferman (1970) and Zygmund (1974). In higher dimensions the conjecture is open, with progress from polynomial partitioning (Guth, 2016) and related methods.

openQuestions.title: The Bochner–Riesz conjecture
openQuestions.q: Do Bochner–Riesz means of a function converge in Lᵖ for the full range of exponents predicted by examples?
openQuestions.known: Carleson and Sjölin (1972) proved the conjecture in two dimensions, and Fefferman’s ball multiplier theorem (1971) shows why the problem is delicate. In three and more dimensions it remains open.

openQuestions.title: Fuglede’s conjecture in low dimensions
openQuestions.q: In one and two dimensions, is a set spectral (admitting an orthogonal basis of exponentials) exactly when it tiles space by translations?
openQuestions.known: Fuglede posed the question in 1974. Tao (2004) disproved it in dimensions five and above, later work extended counterexamples to dimension three, and it is proved for convex sets in every dimension (Lev and Matolcsi, 2022), but dimensions one and two are open.

openQuestions.title: The Pompeiu problem
openQuestions.q: Is the disc the only bounded planar domain for which the Pompeiu property fails?
openQuestions.known: Pompeiu raised the problem in 1929. Its link to an overdetermined eigenvalue problem was found by Williams in the 1970s through what is now called the Schiffer conjecture, and it remains unsolved.

openQuestions.title: Selberg’s eigenvalue conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is the smallest non-zero Laplace eigenvalue on every congruence quotient of the hyperbolic plane at least 1/4?
openQuestions.known: Selberg (1965) proved the bound 3/16. The best known general bound is 975/4096, due to Kim and Sarnak (2003); the full conjecture is a case of the generalised Ramanujan conjecture.

milestones.title: Fourier series
milestones.text: Fourier claims that heat distributions can be written as sums of sines and cosines.

milestones.title: First convergence theorem
milestones.text: Dirichlet gives the first rigorous conditions under which a Fourier series converges to its function.

milestones.title: A divergent Fourier series
milestones.text: Du Bois-Reymond constructs a continuous function whose Fourier series diverges at a point.

milestones.title: Harmonic analysis on groups
milestones.text: The Peter–Weyl theorem extends Fourier series to compact topological groups.

milestones.title: The fast Fourier transform
milestones.text: Cooley and Tukey publish the FFT, making Fourier analysis practical on computers.

milestones.title: Carleson’s theorem
milestones.text: Carleson proves the Fourier series of every square-integrable function converges almost everywhere.

milestones.title: Decoupling
milestones.text: Bourgain, Demeter and Guth use decoupling to prove the main conjecture in Vinogradov’s mean value theorem.

openQuestions.title: The invariant subspace problem
openQuestions.q: Does every bounded operator on a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space have a closed invariant subspace other than zero and the whole space?
openQuestions.known: Enflo (1987) and Read (1985) built operators on certain Banach spaces with no such subspace, but the Hilbert-space case is open. Enflo posted a claimed proof for Hilbert spaces in 2023 that has not been accepted.

openQuestions.title: The Mahler conjecture
openQuestions.q: Among symmetric convex bodies, is the cube (with its dual, the cross-polytope) the one minimising the product of a body’s volume and its dual’s?
openQuestions.known: Mahler proved the plane case in 1939. Iriyeh and Shibata settled three dimensions in 2020; the conjecture is open from dimension four, although Bourgain and Milman (1987) showed it holds up to an exponential factor.

openQuestions.title: Kaplansky’s idempotent and zero-divisor conjectures
openQuestions.q: If a group has no elements of finite order, can its group ring over a field contain zero divisors or non-trivial idempotents?
openQuestions.known: Kaplansky stated these questions in the 1950s and 1970s. His related unit conjecture was disproved by Gardam (2021), but the zero-divisor and idempotent conjectures remain open; the latter follows from the Baum–Connes conjecture for many groups.

openQuestions.title: The free group factor problem
openQuestions.q: Are the von Neumann algebras of the free groups on two and on three generators isomorphic?
openQuestions.known: Murray and von Neumann’s framework makes the question natural, and Voiculescu’s free probability gives powerful tools. Dykema and Rădulescu (1994) showed the free group factors are either all isomorphic or all different, but which holds is unknown.

openQuestions.title: Crouzeix’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is the norm of p(A) always at most twice the maximum of the polynomial p over the numerical range of the matrix A?
openQuestions.known: Crouzeix proposed the constant 2 in 2004 and proved a bound of about 11.08 (2007). Crouzeix and Palencia (2017) improved the constant to 1 + √2, but the conjectured value 2 is unproved.

openQuestions.title: The exact Grothendieck constant
openQuestions.q: What is the exact value of the best constant in Grothendieck’s inequality?
openQuestions.known: Grothendieck proved the inequality in 1953. Krivine (1979) gave the upper bound π/(2 ln(1+√2)) ≈ 1.782 and conjectured it was exact, but Braverman, Makarychev, Makarychev and Naor (2011) showed it is not; the true value is still unknown.

milestones.title: Metric spaces
milestones.text: Fréchet’s thesis introduces abstract metric spaces, letting functions be treated as points.

milestones.title: The Riesz–Fischer theorem
milestones.text: Riesz and Fischer show square-integrable functions form a complete space, the prototype of a Hilbert space.

milestones.title: Banach’s book
milestones.text: Banach’s Théorie des opérations linéaires establishes the theory of complete normed spaces.

milestones.title: Rings of operators
milestones.text: Murray and von Neumann begin the theory of what are now called von Neumann algebras.

milestones.title: C*-algebras
milestones.text: Gelfand and Naimark characterise algebras of operators on Hilbert space abstractly.

milestones.title: The approximation problem
milestones.text: Enflo constructs a Banach space without the approximation property, answering a question from the Scottish Book.

milestones.title: Kadison–Singer
milestones.text: Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava resolve the Kadison–Singer problem using interlacing polynomials.
