openQuestions.title: Quantum unique ergodicity
openQuestions.q: On a compact manifold of negative curvature, do high-energy eigenfunctions of the Laplacian spread out evenly?
openQuestions.known: Rudnick and Sarnak conjectured this in 1994. Lindenstrauss proved it for arithmetic surfaces (2006), and Anantharaman (2008) showed eigenfunctions cannot concentrate too much, but the general conjecture is open.

openQuestions.title: Hearing the shape of a smooth convex drum
openQuestions.q: Is a smooth convex planar domain determined by its Dirichlet eigenvalues?
openQuestions.known: Kac popularised the question in 1966. Gordon, Webb and Wolpert (1992) found different non-convex polygons with the same spectrum, but for smooth convex domains the answer is unknown, apart from results such as Zelditch’s for analytic domains with symmetry.

openQuestions.title: Pólya’s eigenvalue conjecture
openQuestions.q: Are the Dirichlet eigenvalues of every planar domain bounded below by the leading term of Weyl’s law?
openQuestions.known: Pólya proved it for domains that tile the plane (1961). Filonov, Levitin, Polterovich and Sher proved it for the disc in 2023, but it is open for general domains.

openQuestions.title: The Hilbert–Pólya conjecture
openQuestions.q: Are the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function the eigenvalues of some natural self-adjoint operator?
openQuestions.known: The idea is attributed to Hilbert and Pólya around 1914. Montgomery’s pair-correlation results (1973) and Odlyzko’s computations match random-matrix predictions, but no such operator has been found.

openQuestions.title: The Lieb–Thirring constant
openQuestions.q: What is the sharp constant in the Lieb–Thirring inequality for sums of negative eigenvalues of Schrödinger operators?
openQuestions.known: Lieb and Thirring proved the inequality in 1975 to show the stability of matter. Sharp constants are known in some cases, and Frank, Hundertmark, Jex and Nam (2021) gave the best current bounds, but the key three-dimensional case is open.

openQuestions.title: Extended states in the Anderson model
openQuestions.q: In three dimensions, does a weakly disordered random Schrödinger operator have extended states, so that electrons can still conduct?
openQuestions.known: Anderson (1958) predicted localisation at strong disorder, proved by Fröhlich and Spencer (1983) and by Aizenman and Molchanov (1993). Delocalisation at weak disorder is expected physically but is proved only on tree graphs (Klein, 1998); it appears on Barry Simon’s list of open problems (2000).

milestones.title: The Fourier transform
milestones.text: Fourier’s Analytical Theory of Heat represents functions by continuous superpositions of waves.

milestones.title: Fredholm theory
milestones.text: Fredholm develops a theory of integral equations that becomes the model for compact operators.

milestones.title: Weyl’s law
milestones.text: Weyl shows the eigenvalues of the Laplacian grow at a rate fixed by the volume of the domain.

milestones.title: Unbounded self-adjoint operators
milestones.text: Von Neumann proves the spectral theorem for unbounded self-adjoint operators, the setting of quantum mechanics.

milestones.title: Can one hear the shape of a drum?
milestones.text: Kac asks whether a domain is determined by its vibration frequencies.

milestones.title: Isospectral drums
milestones.text: Gordon, Webb and Wolpert construct two different planar domains with identical spectra.

milestones.title: The Ten Martini problem
milestones.text: Avila and Jitomirskaya prove the almost Mathieu operator has a Cantor spectrum for all irrational frequencies.

openQuestions.title: The Kelvin problem
openQuestions.q: How should space be divided into cells of equal volume with the least total wall area?
openQuestions.known: Kelvin proposed a structure of truncated octahedra in 1887. Weaire and Phelan (1993) found a structure with less area, but no partition has been proved optimal.

openQuestions.title: Newton’s minimal resistance problem
openQuestions.q: Which convex body of given height and base meets the least resistance moving through a thin medium?
openQuestions.known: Newton solved it among bodies of revolution in the Principia (1687). Work in the 1990s by Buttazzo, Kawohl and others showed that convex bodies without rotational symmetry can do better, and the true optimum is unknown.

openQuestions.title: The Pólya–Szegő polygon conjecture
openQuestions.q: Among polygons with n sides and fixed area, does the regular polygon have the lowest fundamental frequency?
openQuestions.known: Pólya and Szegő proved it for triangles and quadrilaterals in 1951. It is open for five or more sides, though computer-assisted work supports it.

openQuestions.title: The Thomson problem
openQuestions.q: How should n identical charges arrange themselves on a sphere to minimise their electrostatic energy?
openQuestions.known: J. J. Thomson posed the problem in 1904. Optimal configurations are proved for only a few small values of n, while numerical searches suggest the answers for many more.

openQuestions.title: The moving sofa problem
openQuestions.q: What is the largest area of a shape that can be moved around a right-angled corner in a corridor of unit width?
openQuestions.known: Moser posed it in 1966, and Gerver (1992) found a shape of area about 2.2195. Baek posted a claimed proof in 2024 that Gerver’s sofa is optimal; it is under review.

openQuestions.title: Ulam’s packing conjecture
openQuestions.q: Among convex solids, is the ball the one whose densest packing in space is the least dense?
openQuestions.known: Ulam suggested this in 1972, attributed to a conversation recorded by Gardner. Kallus (2014) showed the ball is a local minimum among centrally symmetric bodies, but the conjecture is open.

milestones.title: The brachistochrone
milestones.text: Johann Bernoulli challenges mathematicians to find the curve of fastest descent, launching the calculus of variations.

milestones.title: Euler’s method
milestones.text: Euler publishes a systematic method for finding curves that extremise integrals, leading to the Euler–Lagrange equation.

milestones.title: Hilbert’s problems
milestones.text: Hilbert’s 19th, 20th and 23rd problems set the agenda for regularity and existence in the calculus of variations.

milestones.title: Plateau’s problem
milestones.text: Douglas and Radó independently prove that every contour in space bounds a minimal surface.

milestones.title: Morse theory
milestones.text: Morse develops variational methods in the large, relating critical points to topology.

milestones.title: Hilbert’s 19th problem
milestones.text: De Giorgi, and independently Nash, prove minimisers of regular variational problems are smooth.

milestones.title: Soap-film geometry
milestones.text: Jean Taylor proves Plateau’s laws describing how soap films meet.

milestones.title: Optimal transport

openQuestions.title: The local Langlands conjectures
openQuestions.q: Are the irreducible representations of a reductive group over a local field classified by arithmetic data called Langlands parameters?
openQuestions.known: Langlands formulated the conjectures in the late 1960s. They are proved for general linear groups (Harris and Taylor; Henniart, 2000–2001), and Fargues and Scholze (2021) attached parameters for all groups, but the full correspondence is open.

openQuestions.title: Arthur’s conjectures
openQuestions.q: Do the automorphic representations occurring in spaces of square-integrable automorphic forms fall into packets with the structure Arthur predicted?
openQuestions.known: Arthur formulated the conjectures in 1989. Arthur himself (2013) established them for symplectic and orthogonal groups, building on the fundamental lemma, but they remain open for general reductive groups.

openQuestions.title: The Dixmier conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is every endomorphism of the Weyl algebra automatically an automorphism?
openQuestions.known: Dixmier asked this in 1968. Tsuchimoto (2005) and independently Belov-Kanel and Kontsevich (2007) showed it is stably equivalent to the Jacobian conjecture, so it is open for the same reasons.

openQuestions.title: The Burnside problem for exponent 5
openQuestions.q: Is the free Burnside group on two generators with exponent 5 finite?
openQuestions.known: Burnside groups are finite for exponents 2, 3, 4 and 6 (Burnside; Sanov, 1940; Hall, 1958), and Novikov and Adian (1968) proved they are infinite for large odd exponents. The case B(2,5) is still open.

openQuestions.title: Zimmer’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: Can a lattice in a higher-rank simple Lie group act non-trivially by diffeomorphisms on a manifold of small dimension?
openQuestions.known: Zimmer proposed the programme in the 1980s, predicting such actions must factor through finite groups. Brown, Fisher and Hurtado (2017 onwards) proved key cases, including cocompact lattices in SL(n,ℝ), but the general conjecture is open.

openQuestions.title: Alperin’s weight conjecture
openQuestions.q: Can the number of modular irreducible characters in a block of a finite group be counted using only local data from its p-subgroups?
openQuestions.known: Alperin proposed the conjecture in 1986. It is known for many families, including p-solvable groups and groups of Lie type in defining characteristic, and has been reduced to a question about simple groups, but it is open in general.

milestones.title: Continuous groups
milestones.text: Lie begins studying continuous transformation groups to solve differential equations.

milestones.title: Classifying simple Lie algebras
milestones.text: Élie Cartan completes Killing’s classification of the complex simple Lie algebras.

milestones.title: Characters of finite groups
milestones.text: Frobenius creates character theory, beginning representation theory of finite groups.

milestones.title: Weyl’s character formula
milestones.text: Weyl computes the characters of irreducible representations of compact Lie groups.

milestones.title: The Langlands programme
milestones.text: Langlands’ letter to Weil proposes deep links between representations and number theory.

milestones.title: Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials
milestones.text: Kazhdan and Lusztig introduce polynomials that govern characters of representations of Lie algebras.

milestones.title: The fundamental lemma
milestones.text: Ngô Bảo Châu proves the fundamental lemma, a key technical step in the Langlands programme.

milestones.title: Geometric Langlands
milestones.text: Gaitsgory, Raskin and collaborators complete a proof of the unramified geometric Langlands conjecture.

openQuestions.title: The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is the number of independent rational points of infinite order on an elliptic curve equal to the order of vanishing of its L-function at s = 1?
openQuestions.known: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer proposed it in the early 1960s from computer experiments; it is a Clay Millennium Problem. Gross–Zagier (1986) and Kolyvagin (1989) proved it when the analytic rank is at most one.

openQuestions.title: The abc conjecture
openQuestions.q: If a + b = c for coprime integers, can c exceed the product of the distinct primes dividing abc by more than a small power, except finitely often?
openQuestions.known: Masser and Oesterlé formulated it in 1985. Mochizuki claimed a proof via inter-universal Teichmüller theory (2012, published 2021), but Scholze and Stix (2018) identified what they regard as a fundamental gap, and the claim is not widely accepted.

openQuestions.title: The inverse Galois problem
openQuestions.q: Does every finite group occur as the Galois group of some extension of the rational numbers?
openQuestions.known: Hilbert showed symmetric and alternating groups occur (1892), and Shafarevich proved it for all solvable groups (1954). Many simple groups are known to occur, but the general problem is open; the Mathieu group M23 is a famous unresolved case.

openQuestions.title: Leopoldt’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is the p-adic regulator of a number field always non-zero?
openQuestions.known: Leopoldt stated the conjecture in 1962. Brumer (1967) proved it for abelian extensions of the rationals and of imaginary quadratic fields using a p-adic form of Baker’s theorem, but it is open in general.

openQuestions.title: The Tate conjecture
openQuestions.q: Over a finitely generated field, are the Galois-invariant cohomology classes on a variety exactly those coming from algebraic cycles?
openQuestions.known: Tate proposed it in 1963 and proved it for divisors on abelian varieties over finite fields (1966). It is known for K3 surfaces over finite fields (Charles; Madapusi Pera; Kim and Madapusi Pera), but open in general.

openQuestions.title: The generalised Ramanujan conjecture
openQuestions.q: Are the local components of cuspidal automorphic representations of GL(n) tempered, so that their Hecke eigenvalues obey Ramanujan’s bound?
openQuestions.known: Deligne (1974) proved Ramanujan’s original conjecture for holomorphic modular forms as a consequence of the Weil conjectures. For Maass forms on GL(2), and in general, it remains open; Kim and Sarnak (2003) gave the best current bound.

milestones.title: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
milestones.text: Gauss’s treatise introduces modular arithmetic and quadratic reciprocity as a systematic theory.

milestones.title: Primes in progressions
milestones.text: Dirichlet proves every suitable arithmetic progression contains infinitely many primes, founding analytic number theory.

milestones.title: Riemann’s zeta function
milestones.text: Riemann links the distribution of primes to the zeros of the zeta function.

milestones.title: The prime number theorem
milestones.text: Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin independently prove the prime number theorem.

milestones.title: Mordell’s conjecture
milestones.text: Faltings proves that a curve of genus at least two has only finitely many rational points.

milestones.title: Fermat’s Last Theorem
milestones.text: Wiles, with Taylor, proves the modularity of semistable elliptic curves and with it Fermat’s Last Theorem.

milestones.title: Primes in arithmetic progression
milestones.text: Green and Tao prove the primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.

milestones.title: Perfectoid spaces
milestones.text: Scholze introduces perfectoid spaces, transforming p-adic geometry.

milestones.title: Bounded gaps between primes
milestones.text: Zhang proves infinitely many pairs of primes differ by less than 70 million; Maynard and Tao soon sharpen the method.

openQuestions.title: Martin’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: Are the natural, definable operations on Turing degrees essentially just iterates of the Turing jump?
openQuestions.known: Martin proposed the conjecture in the 1970s, assuming the axiom of determinacy. Slaman and Steel (1988) proved important special cases, and recent work by Lutz and Siskind settled further parts, but the full conjecture is open.

openQuestions.title: Rigidity of the Turing degrees
openQuestions.q: Does the partial order of Turing degrees have any automorphism other than the identity?
openQuestions.known: Slaman and Woodin showed there are at most countably many automorphisms, and Shore and Slaman (1999) proved the Turing jump is definable from the order. Whether the structure is rigid remains open.

openQuestions.title: The sixth busy beaver number
openQuestions.q: What is the largest number of steps a halting six-state, two-symbol Turing machine can make?
openQuestions.known: Radó introduced the busy beaver function in 1962; it grows faster than any computable function. BB(5) = 47,176,870 was proved in 2024 by the bbchallenge collaboration with a Coq-checked proof, but BB(6) is known only to be astronomically large.

openQuestions.title: The Skolem problem
openQuestions.q: Is there an algorithm that decides whether a linear recurrence sequence of integers ever takes the value zero?
openQuestions.known: The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem (1934–1953) shows the zeros form a periodic set apart from finitely many. Decidability is known for recurrences of order up to four (Mignotte, Shorey and Tijdeman; Vereshchagin, 1985) but open in general.

openQuestions.title: Ordinal analysis of second-order arithmetic
openQuestions.q: Can the proof-theoretic strength of full second-order arithmetic be measured by an explicit ordinal notation?
openQuestions.known: Gentzen gave the ordinal ε₀ for Peano arithmetic (1936), and Takeuti (1967) and later Buchholz, Pohlers and Rathjen analysed much stronger subsystems of second-order arithmetic. A complete ordinal analysis of full second-order arithmetic remains out of reach.

openQuestions.title: Schanuel’s conjecture
openQuestions.q: If n complex numbers are linearly independent over the rationals, do they and their exponentials together contain at least n algebraically independent numbers?
openQuestions.known: Schanuel formulated it in the 1960s. It would settle many transcendence questions; it is not even known whether e + π is irrational. It also implies the decidability of real exponentiation (Macintyre and Wilkie, 1996).

milestones.title: Logic as algebra
milestones.text: Boole’s The Laws of Thought treats logical reasoning as algebraic calculation.

milestones.title: The Entscheidungsproblem
milestones.text: Hilbert and Ackermann ask for an algorithm deciding the validity of any first-order statement.

milestones.title: Consistency of arithmetic
milestones.text: Gentzen proves the consistency of Peano arithmetic by transfinite induction up to ε₀.

milestones.title: Post’s problem
milestones.text: Friedberg and Muchnik independently show there are incomparable computably enumerable Turing degrees.

milestones.title: Type theory
milestones.text: Martin-Löf introduces intuitionistic type theory, a foundation for constructive mathematics and proof assistants.

milestones.title: A natural independent statement
milestones.text: Paris and Harrington find a natural combinatorial statement that is true but unprovable in Peano arithmetic.

milestones.title: The calculus of constructions
milestones.text: Coquand and Huet introduce the calculus of constructions, the basis of the Coq proof assistant.

milestones.title: Univalent foundations
milestones.text: The Homotopy Type Theory book presents univalent foundations linking type theory and homotopy theory.

milestones.title: BB(5) determined
milestones.text: A large online collaboration proves the fifth busy beaver value with a machine-checked proof.

openQuestions.title: Homological mirror symmetry
openQuestions.q: For mirror pairs of Calabi–Yau manifolds, is the Fukaya category of one equivalent to the derived category of coherent sheaves on the other?
openQuestions.known: Kontsevich proposed the conjecture in 1994. It is proved for elliptic curves (Polishchuk and Zaslow, 1998), the quartic K3 surface (Seidel) and several other families, but not in general.

openQuestions.title: The cobordism hypothesis
openQuestions.q: Is a fully extended topological field theory determined by its value on a single point?
openQuestions.known: Baez and Dolan proposed it in 1995. Lurie published a detailed sketch of a proof in 2009, and work on a complete written proof has continued since.

openQuestions.title: The homotopy hypothesis
openQuestions.q: Are higher groupoids, in each proposed model of higher categories, the same thing as topological spaces up to homotopy?
openQuestions.known: Grothendieck formulated the idea in Pursuing Stacks (1983). It holds by construction for Kan complexes, but for several algebraic models of weak higher groupoids it has not been proved.

openQuestions.title: The finitistic dimension conjecture
openQuestions.q: Does every finite-dimensional algebra have finite finitistic global dimension?
openQuestions.known: Bass raised the question around 1960. It is known for many classes, such as monomial algebras and algebras of representation dimension at most three (Igusa and Todorov, 2005), but open in general.

openQuestions.title: Freyd’s generating hypothesis
openQuestions.q: In the stable homotopy category of finite spectra, is a map that induces zero on homotopy groups necessarily zero itself?
openQuestions.known: Freyd posed the conjecture in 1966. It has striking consequences for the structure of the stable homotopy groups of spheres and remains unresolved.

openQuestions.title: Grothendieck’s section conjecture
openQuestions.q: For a hyperbolic curve over a number field, do the sections of its fundamental-group exact sequence correspond exactly to its rational points?
openQuestions.known: Grothendieck stated it in 1983 as part of anabelian geometry. Analogues over p-adic fields and special cases are known, but the conjecture is open.

milestones.title: Categories
milestones.text: Eilenberg and Mac Lane define categories, functors and natural transformations.

milestones.title: Homological algebra
milestones.text: Cartan and Eilenberg’s book makes homological algebra a subject in its own right.

milestones.title: The Tôhoku paper
milestones.text: Grothendieck introduces abelian categories and derived functors in general settings.

milestones.title: Adjoint functors
milestones.text: Kan introduces adjoint functors, now central throughout mathematics.

milestones.title: Derived categories
milestones.text: Verdier, following Grothendieck, develops derived categories.

milestones.title: Model categories
milestones.text: Quillen introduces model categories as a framework for homotopy theory.

milestones.title: Homological mirror symmetry
milestones.text: Kontsevich proposes that mirror symmetry is an equivalence of categories.

milestones.title: Higher topos theory
milestones.text: Lurie publishes Higher Topos Theory, establishing ∞-categories as a working foundation.

openQuestions.title: The Baum–Connes conjecture
openQuestions.q: For a countable group, is the K-theory of its reduced group C*-algebra computed by the assembly map from equivariant K-homology?
openQuestions.known: Baum and Connes formulated it in 1982. It is proved for large classes, including a-T-menable groups (Higson and Kasparov, 2001) and hyperbolic groups (Lafforgue; Mineyev and Yu), while the version with coefficients fails for some groups (Higson, Lafforgue and Skandalis, 2002).

openQuestions.title: The Farrell–Jones conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is the algebraic K-theory of a group ring assembled from the K-theory of its virtually cyclic subgroups?
openQuestions.known: Farrell and Jones proposed it in 1993. It is proved for hyperbolic and CAT(0) groups (Bartels, Lück and Reich) and many others; it implies the Borel and Novikov conjectures for the groups it covers.

openQuestions.title: The Bass conjecture
openQuestions.q: Are the K-groups of a regular ring of finite type over the integers always finitely generated?
openQuestions.known: Bass asked this in the 1960s. It is known in low dimensions, such as for rings of integers in number fields (Quillen, 1973), but is open in general.

openQuestions.title: Vandiver’s conjecture and the K-theory of the integers
openQuestions.q: Does p never divide the class number of the maximal real subfield of the p-th cyclotomic field?
openQuestions.known: Kummer and Vandiver studied the question in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Kurihara (1992) showed it is equivalent to the vanishing of the groups K₄ₙ(ℤ) for all n, linking a classical problem to algebraic K-theory.

openQuestions.title: Beilinson’s conjectures
openQuestions.q: Do special values of L-functions of varieties equal, up to rational factors, regulators built from algebraic K-theory?
openQuestions.known: Beilinson formulated the conjectures in the early 1980s, generalising Borel’s results for number fields. Special cases are known, but the conjectures are largely open.

openQuestions.title: The Bass–Quillen conjecture
openQuestions.q: For a regular ring R, is every finitely generated projective module over a polynomial ring R[x₁,…,xₙ] extended from R?
openQuestions.known: The case where R is a field is the Quillen–Suslin theorem (1976). Lindel proved the conjecture for regular rings essentially of finite type over a field (1981), but it is open in general.

milestones.title: K-theory begins
milestones.text: Grothendieck introduces K-groups of coherent sheaves to prove his Riemann–Roch theorem.

milestones.title: Bott periodicity
milestones.text: Bott proves the homotopy groups of the stable unitary group repeat with period two.

milestones.title: Topological K-theory
milestones.text: Atiyah and Hirzebruch define topological K-theory as an extraordinary cohomology theory.

milestones.title: The index theorem
milestones.text: Atiyah and Singer compute the index of elliptic operators in terms of topology.

milestones.title: Higher algebraic K-theory
milestones.text: Quillen defines higher algebraic K-groups for rings and schemes.

milestones.title: Serre’s problem
milestones.text: Quillen and Suslin independently prove projective modules over polynomial rings over a field are free.

milestones.title: Baum–Connes
milestones.text: Baum and Connes formulate their conjecture linking geometry and operator algebras.

milestones.title: The norm residue theorem
milestones.text: Voevodsky, building on Rost and others, completes the proof of the Bloch–Kato conjecture.

openQuestions.title: The Behrens–Fisher problem
openQuestions.q: How should one test whether two normal populations have equal means when their variances are unknown and may differ?
openQuestions.known: Behrens (1929) and Fisher (1935) posed the problem. Linnik (1966) showed no exact test with natural desirable properties exists, and approximate answers such as Welch’s test are used in practice without a universally accepted solution.

openQuestions.title: Why do overparameterised models generalise?
openQuestions.q: Why can models with far more parameters than data points fit training data exactly yet still predict well?
openQuestions.known: Classical theory predicts overfitting, but Belkin and co-authors (2019) documented double descent in test error. Precise explanations exist for linear and kernel models (for example Bartlett, Long, Lugosi and Tsigler, 2020), but a general theory for deep networks is lacking.

openQuestions.title: Objective Bayesian priors
openQuestions.q: Is there a principled default prior that expresses ignorance about a parameter?
openQuestions.known: Jeffreys (1946) proposed priors invariant under reparameterisation, and Bernardo (1979) introduced reference priors. Different principles give different answers in many models, and there is no agreed general solution.

openQuestions.title: False discovery control under dependence
openQuestions.q: How can the false discovery rate be controlled powerfully when test statistics are arbitrarily dependent?
openQuestions.known: Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) introduced the FDR and a procedure valid for independent tests; Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001) extended it to positive dependence and gave a conservative correction for arbitrary dependence. Sharper general procedures remain an active question.

openQuestions.title: The planted clique problem
openQuestions.q: Can a hidden clique of size much smaller than the square root of n be found in a random graph by an efficient algorithm?
openQuestions.known: Jerrum (1992) and Kučera (1995) introduced the problem; Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov (1998) found cliques of size about √n using spectral methods. It is conjectured no polynomial-time algorithm does better, a benchmark for gaps between statistical and computational limits.

openQuestions.title: Fiducial inference
openQuestions.q: Can Fisher’s fiducial argument be made into a coherent general theory of inference?
openQuestions.known: Fisher introduced fiducial probability in 1930, but it was found to give inconsistent answers in multiparameter problems. Modern variants such as generalised fiducial inference and confidence distributions revive the idea without a settled foundation.

milestones.title: Bayes’ theorem
milestones.text: Bayes’s essay, published posthumously, shows how to update probabilities in the light of data.

milestones.title: Least squares
milestones.text: Legendre publishes the method of least squares for fitting models to observations.

milestones.title: Student’s t-test
milestones.text: Gosset, writing as Student, derives the t-distribution for small samples.

milestones.title: Maximum likelihood
milestones.text: Fisher sets out the mathematical foundations of statistics, including maximum likelihood estimation.

milestones.title: Optimal tests
milestones.text: Neyman and Pearson show how to construct the most powerful test of a hypothesis.

milestones.title: Stein’s paradox
milestones.text: Stein shows the sample mean is inadmissible for estimating three or more normal means.

milestones.title: The bootstrap
milestones.text: Efron introduces the bootstrap, estimating uncertainty by resampling the data.

milestones.title: False discovery rate
milestones.text: Benjamini and Hochberg introduce the false discovery rate for multiple testing.

milestones.title: The lasso
milestones.text: Tibshirani introduces the lasso for sparse regression with many variables.

openQuestions.title: The exponent of matrix multiplication
openQuestions.q: Can two n × n matrices be multiplied using about n² arithmetic operations?
openQuestions.known: Strassen (1969) broke the n³ barrier, and a long line of work has lowered the exponent ω to below 2.372 (Alman, Duan, Vassilevska Williams, Xu, Xu and Zhou, 2024). Whether ω = 2 is open.

openQuestions.title: Why Gaussian elimination is stable in practice
openQuestions.q: Why does Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting almost never suffer the exponential error growth possible in the worst case?
openQuestions.known: Wilkinson (1961) showed the growth factor can be as large as 2ⁿ⁻¹, yet such matrices are almost never met. Trefethen and Schreiber (1990) studied random matrices, and smoothed analysis (Sankar, Spielman and Teng, 2006) gives partial explanations, but a full account is open.

openQuestions.title: A strongly polynomial algorithm for linear programming
openQuestions.q: Is there an algorithm for linear programming whose number of arithmetic steps depends only on the numbers of variables and constraints?
openQuestions.known: Khachiyan (1979) and Karmarkar (1984) gave polynomial-time algorithms whose running time also depends on the size of the numbers. Smale listed the strongly polynomial question as his ninth problem for the 21st century (1998).

openQuestions.title: The polynomial Hirsch conjecture
openQuestions.q: Is the diameter of the graph of every d-dimensional polytope with n facets bounded by a polynomial in n and d?
openQuestions.known: Hirsch’s original bound n − d was disproved by Santos (2010). The best known upper bound, due to Kalai and Kleitman (1992), is quasi-polynomial; a polynomial bound would matter for the simplex method.

openQuestions.title: The great open problem of discrepancy theory
openQuestions.q: How evenly can N points be spread in the d-dimensional unit cube, as measured by star discrepancy?
openQuestions.known: Roth (1954) proved a lower bound of order (log N)^((d−1)/2)/N, while known constructions achieve (log N)^(d−1)/N. Schmidt (1972) settled the two-dimensional case, but the exact order is open in higher dimensions, which affects quasi-Monte Carlo integration.

openQuestions.title: Is the FFT optimal?
openQuestions.q: Does every algorithm for the discrete Fourier transform of length n need on the order of n log n operations?
openQuestions.known: Cooley and Tukey’s FFT (1965) uses O(n log n) operations. Morgenstern (1973) proved a matching lower bound only for restricted linear algorithms with bounded coefficients; no general lower bound is known.

milestones.title: Newton’s method
milestones.text: Newton describes an iterative method for approximating roots of equations, later refined by Raphson.

milestones.title: Gaussian quadrature
milestones.text: Gauss shows how to choose nodes that integrate polynomials of twice the expected degree exactly.

milestones.title: The CFL condition
milestones.text: Courant, Friedrichs and Lewy identify the stability condition for numerical schemes for wave equations.

milestones.title: Conjugate gradients
milestones.text: Hestenes and Stiefel introduce the conjugate gradient method for large linear systems.

milestones.title: The QR algorithm
milestones.text: Francis and Kublanovskaya independently develop the QR algorithm for computing eigenvalues.

milestones.title: Faster matrix multiplication
milestones.text: Strassen shows matrices can be multiplied with fewer than n³ operations.

milestones.title: IEEE 754
milestones.text: The IEEE 754 standard fixes how floating-point arithmetic behaves on computers.

milestones.title: Fast multipole method
milestones.text: Greengard and Rokhlin introduce the fast multipole method for N-body interactions.
